newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO tries to make left-out east Europeans feel in.
newsitem.headline: NATO tries to make left-out east Europeans feel in.

text.p: NATO sought on Friday to reassure disappointed eastern European countries they were part of a new security order despite being excluded from the alliance's first expansion behind the old Iron Curtain.

But it offered no prospects that next month's Madrid summit, which will open NATO's doors for the first time to some former communist eastern and central European states, would set a timetable for bringing in the excluded.

"What NATO ministers stressed today was that the door of the alliance would remain open. Madrid would not be about losers, but winners," NATO Secretary General Javier Solana told a news conference after a two-day meeting of NATO defence ministers.
"My impression, my opinion is that in the (Madrid) communique, there will not be set a particular date, a particular moment, particular names who will be invited to a second wave," he added.

Taking NATO allies by surprise, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen announced on Thursday only Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary should be invited to join the alliance at the July 8-9 summit out of 12 applicants.

As Slovenia and Romania -- who lobbied hard for admission in the first round -- digested the news, NATO defence ministers told the counterparts from 27 "partnership" nations their presence and involvement at NATO headquarters would be increasingly important.
Although the 16 NATO members have to take the decision on who to invite by consensus, Washington carries most weight and Cohen said on Friday he was sure its decision would prevail.
He said he would personally visit Slovenia and Romania "to talk to them to signify to the people that we are serious about the door being open, that this is not just a statement, not just words."

Faced with a smaller expansion than many advocated, NATO defence ministers placed the emphasis on Friday at a meeting with their eastern counterparts on growing links with NATO for 27 partner countries from Azerbaijan to Albania.

The 27, which are joined together in a new body called the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), were invited to set up missions in Brussels and send ambassadors and would be involved from the beginning in peace planning operations.
Solana forecast the NATO work force would double over the next two years to 6,000 from 3,000, putting a strain on the headquarters, which straggle along a suburban Brussels main road.
The reassurances seemed too little for a rejected Slovenia, whose defence minister Turnsek Tit said all countries meeting membership criteria should be invited in.
"If the door is to be open it would be good if it was to open again soon," a NATO official quoted him as saying in reaction to assurances that the first NATO enlargement would not be the last.
Some European partners have vowed to continue pushing the Slovenian and Romanian bids. The two countries have also vowed to try to make President Bill Clinton change his mind.
France and the supporters of a broader expansion argue that the two countries need to be included in order to maintain a balance between NATO's northern and southern flanks.

The NATO and eastern defence ministers also discussed Bosnia and agreed they should do all they could to move towards civilian implementation of the Dayton Peace Accord, but stressed the NATO stabilisation force SFOR could not become a reconstruction agency.
They also discussed relations with Russia after the landmark NATO-Russia partnership accord signed last month in Paris.
